title: MongoDB Wire Protocol
learnerQuestion: Why does MongoDB's wire protocol matter beyond driver internals?
coreClaim: The wire protocol is MongoDB's client/server language boundary and the reason third-party systems can interoperate with MongoDB drivers.
mechanism: Drivers serialize BSON command documents into wire messages and servers return correlated BSON replies.
example: A driver `find()` becomes OP_MSG traffic, not a JavaScript or Python method call.
counterpoint: Wire compatibility does not guarantee command coverage or semantic fidelity.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate MongoDB-compatible systems by wire, command, and semantic contracts.

title: What You Should Be Able To Reason About
learnerQuestion: What should I understand after the deck?
coreClaim: Protocol literacy helps explain OP_MSG, OP_COMPRESSED, BSON commands, handshake negotiation, driver behavior, and compatibility limits.
mechanism: Learning goals move from packet layout to driver behavior and compatibility evaluation.
example: Explain why DocumentDB or FerretDB can use MongoDB drivers but still diverge from MongoDB behavior.
counterpoint: The deck does not replace workload-specific compatibility tests.
practicalTakeaway: Use protocol concepts as the first layer of compatibility analysis.

title: The Wire Protocol Is The Database's Language Boundary
learnerQuestion: What sits between a MongoDB driver and a server?
coreClaim: Drivers and servers communicate through framed messages containing BSON command documents and replies.
mechanism: Client API -> BSON command -> MsgHeader/opcode -> server command dispatcher -> BSON reply.
example: MongoDB, DocumentDB, FerretDB, and Cosmos DB can all expose a MongoDB-driver-facing boundary.
counterpoint: Backends behind that boundary can be very different.
practicalTakeaway: Separate northbound protocol compatibility from backend implementation.

title: A Driver Does Not Send JavaScript Methods; It Sends BSON Commands
learnerQuestion: What actually goes over the socket when application code calls a driver?
coreClaim: Driver APIs compile user operations into BSON command documents.
mechanism: Method arguments become command fields, options, namespaces, sessions, and cursor controls.
example: `collection.find({ status: 'paid' })` becomes a `find` command document.
counterpoint: Driver behavior also depends on topology state, retry options, sessions, and negotiated capabilities.
practicalTakeaway: Debug compatibility at the command document level.

title: Every Message Starts With The Same 16-Byte Header
learnerQuestion: How does a server parse the first bytes of a MongoDB message?
coreClaim: Every MongoDB wire message begins with a four-field message header.
mechanism: `messageLength`, `requestID`, `responseTo`, and `opCode` precede the opcode-specific body.
example: `responseTo` correlates a reply with the original request id.
counterpoint: Header parsing only establishes framing; BSON and command semantics still matter.
practicalTakeaway: A compatible parser starts with length, ids, opcode, and bounds checking.

title: BSON Gives The Wire Protocol Typed Command Documents
learnerQuestion: Why does BSON matter for compatibility?
coreClaim: BSON carries typed command documents and replies, so type semantics are part of protocol compatibility.
mechanism: Fields are serialized with BSON type tags, names, values, and document length framing.
example: ObjectId, Date, Decimal128, Timestamp, binary subtype, and regex behavior can affect results.
counterpoint: JSON-looking commands can lose precision or type meaning if BSON semantics are ignored.
practicalTakeaway: Test BSON type behavior, not only stringified examples.

title: A find Command Becomes A BSON Document Inside OP_MSG
learnerQuestion: What does a normal read look like as a command?
coreClaim: Modern reads use command documents carried in OP_MSG sections.
mechanism: OP_MSG section kind 0 carries the command body with fields such as `find`, `filter`, `sort`, `limit`, and `$db`.
example: { find: 'orders', filter: { status: 'paid' }, '$db': 'shop' }.
counterpoint: The actual command may include sessions, read concern, comments, API version, or driver-added fields.
practicalTakeaway: Look at command documents when diagnosing driver/server behavior.

title: The Protocol Moved From Operation Opcodes To Command Transport
learnerQuestion: Why did MongoDB move toward OP_MSG?
coreClaim: Command documents became the extensible center of protocol evolution as MongoDB added richer distributed features.
mechanism: Legacy operation bodies gave way to command documents and OP_MSG sections.
example: Sessions, retryable writes, transactions, read concern, and write concern fit naturally as command fields.
counterpoint: Legacy opcodes still matter historically and for older compatibility contexts.
practicalTakeaway: Understand OP_MSG as the modern baseline.

title: The Original Opcodes Encoded Database Operations Directly
learnerQuestion: What did the older protocol messages encode?
coreClaim: Legacy opcodes such as OP_QUERY, OP_INSERT, OP_UPDATE, OP_DELETE, OP_GET_MORE, and OP_KILL_CURSORS encoded operations in specialized bodies.
mechanism: Each opcode had its own fields, flags, namespace, and document payload shape.
example: OP_QUERY used namespace and query selector fields rather than an OP_MSG command body.
counterpoint: MongoDB deprecated several older formats in favor of OP_MSG.
practicalTakeaway: Legacy opcode support is not the same as modern MongoDB compatibility.

title: Feature Growth Did Not Fit Operation-Specific Message Bodies
learnerQuestion: Why not keep adding flags to old message formats?
coreClaim: Operation-specific message bodies were less extensible than command documents for feature growth.
mechanism: Command fields can carry options, sessions, transaction numbers, read/write concern, and API metadata uniformly.
example: Transaction context rides as command fields rather than a bespoke opcode body.
counterpoint: Extensibility shifts complexity into command semantics and compatibility testing.
practicalTakeaway: Expect modern features to appear as command fields.

title: Before OP_MSG, Commands Rode Through $cmd
learnerQuestion: How were commands sent before OP_MSG became the command-native envelope?
coreClaim: Before OP_MSG, commands could be transported through command namespaces such as `$cmd` using OP_QUERY.
mechanism: A command document was placed inside an OP_QUERY-style request to a command namespace.
example: Early command traffic used `$cmd` as a bridge between query transport and command semantics.
counterpoint: This is primarily historical context for understanding compatibility evolution.
practicalTakeaway: Do not confuse command semantics with the transport envelope used to carry them.

title: OP_MSG Is The Modern Command-Native Envelope
learnerQuestion: What makes OP_MSG the modern protocol shape?
coreClaim: OP_MSG is a bidirectional envelope for command request and reply documents.
mechanism: OP_MSG has flags and typed sections, including body and document sequence sections.
example: A command body plus a document sequence for bulk inserts.
counterpoint: The envelope is simple compared with the semantic complexity inside command fields.
practicalTakeaway: Parse OP_MSG sections before interpreting command semantics.

title: OP_MSG Separates Command Body From Bulk Document Sequences
learnerQuestion: How does OP_MSG carry large batches efficiently?
coreClaim: OP_MSG can separate the command body from a document sequence so bulk payloads do not need to be nested into one huge BSON command document.
mechanism: Section kind 1 identifies a sequence name followed by a list of BSON documents.
example: Bulk insert documents can be sent as a sequence associated with the `documents` field.
counterpoint: Servers still need command-specific validation and size-limit enforcement.
practicalTakeaway: Treat OP_MSG section kind as part of command parsing.

title: Bulk Writes Avoid Nesting Every Document Inside One Huge Command BSON
learnerQuestion: Why does OP_MSG need document sequences?
coreClaim: Document sequences support bulk payloads while preserving command metadata in the body.
mechanism: The command body names the operation; sequence sections carry repeated documents.
example: Insert command metadata in body, inserted documents in a sequence.
counterpoint: Bulk compatibility still depends on ordered/unordered, errors, write concern, and result document semantics.
practicalTakeaway: Bulk support is packet layout plus result semantics.

title: Replies Are Also Command Documents
learnerQuestion: What does the server send back?
coreClaim: Replies are BSON command documents with status, cursor data, errors, and metadata.
mechanism: Response messages correlate by header id and carry documents such as `{ ok: 1, cursor: ... }`.
example: A `find` reply contains a cursor id, namespace, and first batch.
counterpoint: Compatible systems must match error labels and result shapes, not only ok/error booleans.
practicalTakeaway: Reply shape influences driver cursor and retry behavior.

title: The First Conversation Negotiates Topology And Capabilities
learnerQuestion: What happens before application commands run?
coreClaim: Drivers handshake to discover topology, server capabilities, wire versions, compressors, and metadata behavior.
mechanism: Driver sends hello/handshake command; server replies with topology and capability fields.
example: `maxWireVersion`, `isWritablePrimary`, `hosts`, and compressor-related fields affect driver state.
counterpoint: A compatible server can pass connection tests but still fail later command semantics.
practicalTakeaway: Handshake correctness is a prerequisite for driver trust.

title: minWireVersion And maxWireVersion Are Feature Gates
learnerQuestion: How do drivers know which protocol features are legal?
coreClaim: Wire versions are negotiated feature gates, distinct from product version and Stable API version.
mechanism: Hello responses include min and max wire versions that drivers compare against supported ranges.
example: OP_MSG availability is tied to MongoDB 3.6-era wire version support.
counterpoint: A high wire version claim is risky if command semantics do not match that capability.
practicalTakeaway: Do not treat wire version as full API compatibility.

title: OP_COMPRESSED Wraps Another Complete Wire Message
learnerQuestion: Is compression a different command model?
coreClaim: OP_COMPRESSED is a transport wrapper around another complete MongoDB wire message.
mechanism: Wrapper contains original opcode, uncompressed size, compressor id, and compressed message bytes.
example: An OP_COMPRESSED packet can wrap an OP_MSG command.
counterpoint: After decompression, the original opcode and payload still need normal parsing.
practicalTakeaway: Decompress first, then parse the enclosed original message.

title: Compression Is Opt-In And Per-Connection
learnerQuestion: When can a driver compress wire messages?
coreClaim: Compression is negotiated per connection using mutually supported compressors.
mechanism: Handshake negotiation chooses supported compressors such as snappy, zlib, or zstd where available.
example: A driver configured with zstd can use it only if the server advertises support.
counterpoint: Compression trades CPU for fewer bytes and is workload-dependent.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate compression by payload size, CPU, latency, and network cost.

title: A Proxy Or Compatible Server Starts By Decoding The Header
learnerQuestion: What does a MongoDB-compatible proxy need to do first?
coreClaim: A compatible implementation must safely decode headers, opcodes, BSON bodies, compression wrappers, and request correlation.
mechanism: Read length -> validate bounds -> parse header -> handle OP_COMPRESSED if present -> parse OP_MSG/legacy body -> dispatch command.
example: FerretDB receives MongoDB wire protocol queries before translating to SQL-backed execution.
counterpoint: Correct parsing is necessary but far easier than semantic fidelity.
practicalTakeaway: Byte parsing is the first compatibility layer, not the last.

title: After The Header, Parse Flags And Section Kinds
learnerQuestion: What makes OP_MSG parsing more than just BSON decoding?
coreClaim: OP_MSG contains flags and sections that control how command bodies and sequences are interpreted.
mechanism: Parser reads message flags, then section kind 0 bodies or section kind 1 document sequences.
example: A bulk write may include command metadata in body and repeated documents in a sequence.
counterpoint: Malformed section lengths or unexpected section names must be rejected safely.
practicalTakeaway: Treat OP_MSG structure as a first-class parser contract.

title: A Driver Turns API Calls Into Protocol Work Plus Topology State
learnerQuestion: Why is a MongoDB driver more than a serializer?
coreClaim: Drivers combine command construction with server discovery, selection, sessions, retryability, cursor state, and capability checks.
mechanism: API call -> topology state -> command construction -> wire message -> reply parsing -> state update.
example: A `find` may target primary or secondary depending on read preference and topology.
counterpoint: Compatible servers must provide enough topology metadata for drivers to make correct decisions.
practicalTakeaway: Test with real drivers, not only raw socket clients.

title: Queries Often Become Multiple Wire Round Trips
learnerQuestion: Why can one query produce more than one message exchange?
coreClaim: Cursor-bearing commands return initial batches and may require getMore traffic for remaining results.
mechanism: Reply includes cursor id and firstBatch; driver sends follow-up getMore commands until cursor exhaustion or close.
example: A dashboard query returning many orders may issue multiple getMore requests.
counterpoint: Batch size and cursor behavior affect latency, memory, and compatibility.
practicalTakeaway: Measure round trips and cursor behavior in compatibility/performance tests.

title: Modern Distributed Semantics Ride As Command Fields
objective: Explain command fields for distributed behavior.
learnerQuestion: Where do sessions, transactions, and retryability appear on the wire?
coreClaim: Modern distributed semantics are encoded in command fields inside OP_MSG command documents.
mechanism: Commands may carry lsid, txnNumber, autocommit, readConcern, writeConcern, apiVersion, and related fields.
example: Retryable write metadata rides with the command document.
counterpoint: Parsing fields is not enough; server behavior must match the semantics implied by those fields.
practicalTakeaway: Compatibility must test command fields and their effects.

title: Auth Is Also Command Traffic Over The Same Channel
learnerQuestion: Is authentication separate from the wire protocol?
coreClaim: Authentication is command traffic over the same connection and protocol framing.
mechanism: SCRAM/SASL flows exchange authentication commands and responses after connection/handshake setup.
example: A driver authenticates before issuing application commands.
counterpoint: TLS, auth mechanisms, and credential sources add deployment-specific constraints.
practicalTakeaway: Include auth mechanisms in compatibility tests.

title: The Wire Protocol Also Carries Deployment Topology Signals
learnerQuestion: How does a driver learn whether it is talking to a primary, secondary, or router?
coreClaim: Topology signals are reported through hello/SDAM command replies.
mechanism: Hello fields drive driver topology descriptions, server selection, monitoring, and retry behavior.
example: Replica set hosts and writable primary signals affect where writes are routed.
counterpoint: Incorrect topology metadata can break otherwise valid command parsing.
practicalTakeaway: Topology compatibility is part of protocol compatibility.

title: Drivers Trust The Protocol Boundary, Not The Storage Engine
learnerQuestion: Why can a non-MongoDB backend use MongoDB drivers?
coreClaim: Drivers trust the wire, command, and response contracts rather than the backend storage engine.
mechanism: A server can parse messages, execute commands, and return MongoDB-shaped replies using any internal storage model.
example: FerretDB translates wire protocol traffic to PostgreSQL-backed execution.
counterpoint: Driver trust becomes dangerous if semantic behavior only partly matches MongoDB.
practicalTakeaway: Ask what the driver can observe, not what backend is hidden.

title: Wire-Compatible Is Necessary But Not Sufficient
learnerQuestion: What does wire-compatible fail to prove?
coreClaim: Wire compatibility proves the driver can talk; it does not prove command coverage, semantic fidelity, or operational equivalence.
mechanism: Layered compatibility: wire framing -> command syntax -> result semantics -> operational behavior.
example: A server may accept `aggregate` but differ on stages, limits, transactions, or indexes.
counterpoint: For simple workloads, partial compatibility may be enough.
practicalTakeaway: Define the workload's required compatibility layer.

title: Who Speaks Enough Of The MongoDB Protocol To Use MongoDB Clients?
learnerQuestion: Which technologies use MongoDB-compatible client surfaces?
coreClaim: MongoDB-compatible systems span managed API-compatible services, translation layers, PostgreSQL-backed engines, and MongoDB-derived server distributions.
mechanism: Each exposes a northbound MongoDB-driver-facing contract with different backend architecture.
example: Amazon DocumentDB, FerretDB, Cosmos DB for MongoDB, Microsoft DocumentDB, and Percona Server for MongoDB.
counterpoint: Compatibility depth varies by product version and feature area.
practicalTakeaway: Compare compatible systems by architecture and supported workload, not name alone.

title: Other Compatibility Layers Follow The Same Northbound Pattern
learnerQuestion: What do these systems have in common?
coreClaim: Compatible systems keep the MongoDB client contract northbound while changing storage, scaling, or operations southbound.
mechanism: Driver-facing parser and command engine mediate between MongoDB commands and backend-specific execution.
example: A PostgreSQL-backed implementation maps document commands onto SQL/document storage internals.
counterpoint: Northbound similarity can hide major operational differences.
practicalTakeaway: Draw northbound and southbound contracts separately.

title: DocumentDB Demonstrates Protocol Compatibility Without MongoDB Internals
learnerQuestion: How can Amazon DocumentDB use MongoDB drivers without being MongoDB?
coreClaim: Amazon DocumentDB exposes MongoDB API compatibility with version-specific supported features and syntax.
mechanism: It implements enough MongoDB-compatible protocol/API behavior for targeted driver workloads while documenting compatibility differences.
example: AWS publishes compatibility matrices by MongoDB API area and engine version.
counterpoint: Compatibility matrices must be checked before migration because unsupported features can be material.
practicalTakeaway: Read the compatibility matrix before assuming MongoDB equivalence.

title: FerretDB Is A Protocol Translation Layer Over PostgreSQL
learnerQuestion: How does FerretDB make MongoDB drivers work with PostgreSQL-backed storage?
coreClaim: FerretDB acts as a proxy that converts MongoDB 5.0+ wire protocol queries to SQL over PostgreSQL with DocumentDB extension.
mechanism: MongoDB driver -> MongoDB wire protocol -> FerretDB proxy -> SQL/PostgreSQL-backed document engine -> MongoDB-shaped reply.
example: A MongoDB-compatible app connects to FerretDB using normal MongoDB drivers.
counterpoint: FerretDB documents compatibility limits; translation does not guarantee full MongoDB semantics.
practicalTakeaway: Translation architecture makes semantic coverage the hard part.

title: MongoDB API Services Expose Driver-Compatible Endpoints
learnerQuestion: How do managed services reuse MongoDB drivers and tools?
coreClaim: Managed MongoDB API services expose MongoDB wire protocol endpoints so existing drivers, SDKs, and tools can connect.
mechanism: Service endpoint accepts MongoDB driver connections and maps commands onto provider-specific storage and operations.
example: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB supports MongoDB wire protocol for existing drivers and tools.
counterpoint: Provider consistency, partitioning, indexing, pricing, and feature support can differ from MongoDB.
practicalTakeaway: Treat driver compatibility as onboarding convenience, not complete migration proof.

title: PostgreSQL-Backed MongoDB Compatibility Is Becoming A Broader Pattern
learnerQuestion: Why do several compatibility efforts use PostgreSQL?
coreClaim: PostgreSQL-backed document compatibility is emerging as a pattern for exposing MongoDB-like APIs over relational infrastructure.
mechanism: BSON/document storage extensions and command translators map document operations onto PostgreSQL-based execution.
example: Microsoft DocumentDB and FerretDB's PostgreSQL-backed direction.
counterpoint: A PostgreSQL backend changes scaling, transaction, index, and operational assumptions.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate backend architecture, not just the MongoDB-facing API.

title: A Compatible Implementation Is Often A Wire-Protocol Proxy Plus Command Engine
learnerQuestion: What components must a compatible implementation build?
coreClaim: A compatible implementation needs wire parsing, command dispatch, semantic execution, backend adapters, response mapping, and observability.
mechanism: Packet parser -> BSON decoder -> command router -> semantic engine -> backend adapter -> response/error mapper.
example: A `find` command may translate to an internal query plan and then return a MongoDB-shaped cursor reply.
counterpoint: The parser is usually the easy layer compared with semantic behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Ask which layer a compatibility failure belongs to.

title: The Hard Part Is Semantic Fidelity, Not Parsing Bytes
learnerQuestion: Why do compatible systems still surprise applications?
coreClaim: Applications depend on command behavior, operator semantics, errors, consistency, performance, and limits beyond byte parsing.
mechanism: Semantic fidelity includes operators, aggregation stages, indexes, transactions, sessions, cursor behavior, and error labels.
example: Two systems may both parse `aggregate` but diverge on supported stages or memory limits.
counterpoint: For constrained workloads, a smaller command subset can be viable.
practicalTakeaway: Build compatibility tests around real application behavior.

title: Where MongoDB-Compatible Systems Most Often Diverge
learnerQuestion: What should migration tests target first?
coreClaim: Common divergence areas include unsupported commands, aggregation semantics, transactions, indexes, change streams, auth, performance, and operations.
mechanism: Different backends implement subsets or alternative semantics for MongoDB command surfaces.
example: DocumentDB and FerretDB maintain explicit compatibility documentation.
counterpoint: Divergence is product-version-specific and changes over time.
practicalTakeaway: Test the hardest commands first, not only CRUD.

title: Wire Version, API Version, And Product Version Are Different Things
learnerQuestion: Which version number matters for compatibility?
coreClaim: Wire version gates protocol features, Stable API version constrains command/API behavior, and product version identifies a server or service release.
mechanism: Drivers read wire versions from hello; applications can request Stable API behavior; products publish compatibility matrices.
example: A compatible service may advertise a MongoDB API level without matching every MongoDB product feature.
counterpoint: Version claims must be verified against actual command support and behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Always ask which compatibility version is being discussed.

title: Wire Compatibility Expands The Blast Radius Of Driver Behavior
objective: Explain why driver behavior matters for compatible systems.
learnerQuestion: How can a driver assumption break a compatible server?
coreClaim: Drivers infer capabilities and topology from protocol responses, so incorrect compatibility signals can amplify failures.
mechanism: Hello fields, wire versions, error labels, cursor ids, sessions, and retryability shape driver decisions.
example: A server advertising unsupported wire features may trigger driver code paths it cannot satisfy.
counterpoint: Conservative capability reporting can reduce risk but may limit feature access.
practicalTakeaway: Compatible servers should advertise only capabilities they can uphold.

title: The Protocol Has Real Performance Consequences
learnerQuestion: How can protocol details affect latency and throughput?
coreClaim: Message size, compression, batching, cursor round trips, and command shape affect performance.
mechanism: Payload size, compressor choice, document sequence use, batchSize, getMore count, and network round trips interact.
example: Small batches can create extra getMore round trips; large payloads may benefit from compression.
counterpoint: Backend execution often dominates protocol overhead for complex queries.
practicalTakeaway: Measure wire round trips and payload sizes alongside query latency.

title: Useful Protocol-Level Signals To Capture
learnerQuestion: What should I log or trace at the protocol layer?
coreClaim: Protocol observability should capture command names, opcodes, wire versions, sizes, compression, round trips, cursor ids, errors, and topology metadata.
mechanism: Trace request/reply metadata without exposing sensitive command payloads unnecessarily.
example: Record opcode distribution, message length, command name, error labels, and response time.
counterpoint: Payload logging can expose credentials or sensitive data and must be governed.
practicalTakeaway: Collect enough protocol metadata to debug compatibility safely.

title: How To Evaluate A MongoDB-Compatible Technology
learnerQuestion: What should an evaluation cover beyond a connection test?
coreClaim: Evaluation must cover wire, command, semantic, performance, operational, tooling, and migration behavior.
mechanism: Test matrix maps application workload commands to documented support and measured behavior.
example: Run CRUD, aggregation, index, transaction, auth, change stream, and failover tests for the real workload.
counterpoint: Some compatibility gaps may be acceptable if the workload never uses those surfaces.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate compatibility by workload, not by product slogan.

title: The Wire Protocol Lowers Switching Cost, But Does Not Erase It
learnerQuestion: What migration friction remains after driver compatibility?
coreClaim: Driver reuse lowers migration friction, but unsupported commands, semantics, performance, and operations can still require application work.
mechanism: Wire compatibility preserves connection and driver API paths while semantic and operational layers may diverge.
example: A tool can connect, but a production aggregation or transaction may fail or behave differently.
counterpoint: For simple CRUD workloads, the remaining friction may be modest.
practicalTakeaway: Plan migration testing around the highest-risk semantics.

title: The Protocol Created An Ecosystem Boundary
learnerQuestion: Why has the protocol enabled third-party systems?
coreClaim: A stable driver-facing protocol allows third-party systems to reuse MongoDB drivers, tools, and application code paths.
mechanism: Providers implement northbound protocol and command behavior while innovating on backend storage, licensing, scale, or operations.
example: DocumentDB, FerretDB, Cosmos DB for MongoDB, and Microsoft DocumentDB all leverage this boundary differently.
counterpoint: Ecosystem reuse depends on sufficient command and semantic coverage.
practicalTakeaway: Protocol standardization creates an interface market.

title: Think In Three Contracts
learnerQuestion: What mental model should I use for compatibility?
coreClaim: Compatibility should be evaluated as wire contract, command contract, and semantic contract.
mechanism: Wire contract: can driver talk; command contract: can app express work; semantic contract: does it behave the same.
example: A system may satisfy wire and basic commands but fail semantic requirements for transactions.
counterpoint: Operational contract is often a fourth practical layer for production decisions.
practicalTakeaway: Name the contract that is being tested or claimed.

title: What The Wire Protocol Explains
learnerQuestion: What does protocol knowledge explain well?
coreClaim: Protocol knowledge explains driver/server mechanics, OP_MSG evolution, OP_COMPRESSED wrapping, BSON payloads, and interoperability boundaries.
mechanism: Message header, opcode, BSON command, sections, compression wrapper, handshake, reply documents, and cursor traffic.
example: A driver can connect to a compatible server because the northbound message contract is recognizable.
counterpoint: Protocol knowledge does not by itself predict full query semantics or operational behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Use protocol knowledge as the first layer of system reasoning.

title: How To Reason About MongoDB-Compatible Systems
learnerQuestion: What should I remember when evaluating compatibility?
coreClaim: Wire compatibility is the beginning of evaluation; production migration requires semantic, operational, and tooling tests.
mechanism: Layered testing from connection and command execution through workload results, failover behavior, observability, and operations.
example: Run the real app's aggregations, transactions, indexes, auth flows, and failure scenarios.
counterpoint: A constrained workload can tolerate constrained compatibility if risks are explicit.
practicalTakeaway: Require workload-specific proof before migration.

title: Follow-up Reading
learnerQuestion: Where should I verify protocol and compatibility details?
coreClaim: MongoDB manual and driver specifications define protocol mechanics; product docs define compatibility coverage for third-party systems.
mechanism: References are grouped by wire protocol/BSON, drivers/handshake, and compatible technologies.
example: Use MongoDB wire protocol docs for packet layout and AWS/FerretDB/Microsoft docs for product compatibility.
counterpoint: Compatibility pages change with product releases and must be checked when making decisions.
practicalTakeaway: Validate current compatibility against current primary docs.
